findings.title: Removed fail-fast check for multiple CryptoProviders on classpath, now silently resolved with non-deterministic tie-breaking
findings.body: Previously detectProvider() threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classloader, which protected against misconfiguration (e.g. accidentally having both a FIPS and a non-FIPS provider on the classpath, which has real compliance/security implications). Now the providers are simply sorted by order() and the highest-order one is silently picked, logging the rest only at debug level (logger.debugf, line ~69). If two providers happen to have the same order() value (e.g. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all use order()==200), the choice between them depends on ServiceLoader enumeration order, which is unspecified and can vary across JVMs/classloaders. This can silently select a FIPS or non-FIPS provider unintentionally, with no error raised and only a debug-level log that is typically not visible in production, defeating the original safety check.

findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks binary/source compatibility for existing CryptoProvider implementors
findings.body: The interface CryptoProvider now declares `int order();` as an abstract method with no default implementation. Any existing third-party or custom implementation of CryptoProvider (e.g. custom SPI providers maintained outside this PR) will fail to compile/load until updated to implement order(). Since CryptoProvider is a public SPI loaded via ServiceLoader, this is a breaking API change that should either provide a default method (e.g. default int order() { return 0; }) or be called out explicitly as a breaking change in release notes.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() does not return a BouncyCastle provider, violating the interface contract
findings.body: CryptoProvider#getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented as returning 'BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider'. This implementation instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is simply whatever JCA provider implements the platform default keystore type (e.g. the JDK's built-in PKCS12 provider), not BouncyCastle at all. Any caller relying on the documented contract (e.g. to register BC-specific algorithms, or pass 'BC' as a provider name) will get unexpected/incorrect behavior rather than a clear UnsupportedOperationException like the rest of the unimplemented methods in this class.

findings.title: Dead code: throwaway ASN1Encoder instances created and discarded
findings.body: In concatenatedRSToASN1DER(), lines 114-115 create two separate ASN1Encoder instances and call write(rBigInteger)/write(sBigInteger) on them, but the results are never used (new encoders are created again a few lines later to actually build the returned bytes). This is dead code left over from development that performs unnecessary work on every signature conversion and is confusing to maintain; it should be removed.

findings.title: AuthzClient.create() triggers global static CryptoIntegration initialization as a side effect
findings.body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). CryptoIntegration keeps a process-wide static singleton (cryptoProvider) that, once set, cannot be changed except via explicit setProvider(). If AuthzClient.create() is invoked before the hosting application performs its own CryptoIntegration.init() (e.g. when authz-client is embedded inside a larger application/server that shares the same classloader or class-loading hierarchy), the singleton can get permanently locked to whatever CryptoProvider is visible to AuthzClient's classloader at that moment — potentially the minimal AuthzClientCryptoProvider, which throws UnsupportedOperationException for almost every operation except order(), getBouncyCastleProvider(), getEcdsaCryptoProvider() and getKeyStore(). Any later, unrelated code path in the same classloader that needs other crypto features (PEM utils, certificate utils, key generation, etc.) would then fail with UnsupportedOperationException instead of using the application's intended full-featured provider.

findings.title: No test coverage for the new multi-provider ordering/tie-breaking logic
findings.body: This PR introduces a significant behavioral change to CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(): instead of failing when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are found, it now sorts by CryptoProvider.order() and silently picks the highest. No unit test is added anywhere in the diff to verify this sorting logic, the tie-breaking behavior when two providers share the same order value, or that a provider is correctly ignored/logged. Given this is core logic that determines which cryptographic backend the whole application uses, it should have direct test coverage.
